title: Vector as a Stack, and Capacity
summary: A vector has a **size** (elements in use) and a **capacity** (room reserved). When it runs out of room it reallocates. `push_back`, `pop_back` and `back` make it a natural **stack**: last in, first out.
markdown:
## Size and capacity A vector usually reserves more room than it is using, so that adding an element does not always require new memory. ``` size is 3 capacity is 4 ┌──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐ │ 10 │ 20 │ 30 │ │ one slot reserved, not yet in use └──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘ ``` | | Meaning | |---|---| | `v.size()` | How many elements it holds | | `v.capacity()` | How many it could hold before needing more memory | ## Reallocation When the capacity is used up, the next `push_back` cannot extend the block in place. The vector **reallocates**: ```mermaid flowchart LR A["old block, capacity 4
10 20 30 40"] -->|"1. allocate a larger block"| B["new block, capacity 8"] B -->|"2. move the elements across"| C["10 20 30 40 _ _ _ _"] C -->|"3. add 50, release the old block"| D["10 20 30 40 50 _ _ _"] ``` Each reallocation grows the capacity by a factor (1.5 with Microsoft's compiler, 2 with most others), so reallocations become rarer as the vector grows. Averaged over many calls, `push_back` takes constant time. The term for that is **amortized constant time**. ```cpp #include #include int main() { std::vector v{}; for (int i{ 0 }; i < 10; ++i) { v.push_back(i); std::cout << "size " << v.size() << " capacity " << v.capacity() << '\n'; } return 0; } ``` > [!danger] Reallocation invalidates everything that points into the vector > After a reallocation the elements live at new addresses. Any pointer, reference or iterator to an element obtained earlier now refers to released memory. > ```cpp > int& first{ v[0] }; > v.push_back(99); // may reallocate > first = 1; // undefined behaviour if it did > ``` > This is called **invalidation**, and it is one of the most common sources of subtle bugs in C++. ## `reserve` and `resize` | | `reserve(n)` | `resize(n)` | |---|---|---| | Changes the size | No | Yes, to `n` | | Changes the capacity | To at least `n` | Only if needed | | Creates elements | No | Yes, with default values | | Use it when | You are about to `push_back` roughly `n` elements | You want `n` elements to exist now | ```cpp std::vector v{}; v.reserve(1000); // one allocation, done in advance for (int i{ 0 }; i < 1000; ++i) { v.push_back(i); // never reallocates } ``` When you know roughly how many elements are coming, `reserve` is a free speed-up. It also guarantees that no invalidation happens during the fill. ## A vector as a stack A **stack** is a collection where you add and remove at the same end. The last item in is the first out, abbreviated **LIFO**. ``` push 1 push 2 push 3 pop ┌───┐ ┌───┐ ┌───┐ ┌───┐ │ │ │ │ │ 3 │ top │ │ │ │ │ 2 │ top │ 2 │ │ 2 │ top │ 1 │ top │ 1 │ │ 1 │ │ 1 │ └───┘ └───┘ └───┘ └───┘ ``` The end of a vector is exactly where adding and removing are cheap. | Stack operation | Vector call | |---|---| | Push | `v.push_back(x)` | | Look at the top | `v.back()` | | Pop | `v.pop_back()` | | Is it empty? | `v.empty()` | ```cpp #include #include int main() { std::vector stack{}; stack.push_back(1); stack.push_back(2); stack.push_back(3); std::cout << stack.back() << '\n'; // 3 stack.pop_back(); std::cout << stack.back() << '\n'; // 2 return 0; } ``` > [!warning] `pop_back` returns nothing > Read `back()` first if you need the value. And both `back()` and `pop_back()` on an empty vector are undefined behaviour, so check `empty()` first. Stacks are everywhere: undo history, matching brackets, evaluating expressions, backtracking through a maze. The mechanism that tracks your own function calls is a stack too. The library also offers `std::stack` in ``, a thin wrapper with `push`, `pop` and `top`. ## `emplace_back` `push_back` takes a finished element and puts it in. `emplace_back` takes the **ingredients** and builds the element directly inside the vector. ```cpp struct Point { int x{}; int y{}; }; std::vector points{}; points.push_back({ 1, 2 }); // build a Point, then move it in points.emplace_back(3, 4); // build it in place ``` For simple types the difference is negligible. It matters for elements that are expensive to construct. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What does `pop_back()` return? - The removed element - The new last element + Nothing - The new size of the vector > `pop_back()` returns `void`. Read `back()` first if you need the value. ? Why can a reference to `v[0]` become invalid after `push_back`? + If the capacity is exceeded, the vector moves every element to new memory and releases the old block - Because `push_back` always inserts the new element at index 0 - Because references to vector elements last only until the next statement - Because `push_back` sorts the vector > Growing beyond the capacity means a new, bigger block. The old one is released, so references into it dangle. ? What is the difference between `reserve(100)` and `resize(100)`? - There is none - `resize` only sets aside room; `reserve` adds 100 elements + `reserve` only sets aside room; `resize` adds 100 elements - `reserve` frees memory; `resize` allocates it > `reserve` changes the capacity only. After `resize(100)`, `size()` is 100 and you can index all of them. ? What does LIFO mean? - Least important, first out - Loop in, finish once - Last in, final out: elements are never removed + Last in, first out: the most recently added element is removed first > A stack is LIFO: `push_back` adds to the top and `pop_back` removes from the top. ```
ideas:
1. Print the size and capacity while pushing 20 elements. What growth factor do you see?
2. Use a vector as a stack to check whether brackets are balanced: `{[()()]}` is, `([)]` is not.
3. Reverse a string using a stack.

cards.a:
Nothing

`pop_back()` returns `void`. Read `back()` first if you need the value.

cards.q: Why can a reference to `v[0]` become invalid after `push_back`?
cards.a:
If the capacity is exceeded, the vector moves every element to new memory and releases the old block

Growing beyond the capacity means a new, bigger block. The old one is released, so references into it dangle.

cards.q: What is the difference between `reserve(100)` and `resize(100)`?
cards.a:
`reserve` only sets aside room; `resize` adds 100 elements

`reserve` changes the capacity only. After `resize(100)`, `size()` is 100 and you can index all of them.

Last in, first out: the most recently added element is removed first

A stack is LIFO: `push_back` adds to the top and `pop_back` removes from the top.
